papers.title: Solar System Surface Technosignatures: Searching for Signs of Artificial Design on Extraterrestrial Terrain
papers.abstract: Artificial radio emissions have historically been a major focus of technosignature searches. Here, we apply an anthropological lens to expand this scope to surface technosignatures: non-random, intentional patterning on planetary terrain, similar to long-lasting human-made landscapes and monuments on Earth. On geologically inactive bodies such as the Moon and Mars, artificial traces and patterns could potentially remain visible for hundreds of millions of years. We discuss two recent developments that make this search timely: high-resolution imaging datasets, such as those produced by the HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and ML-based anomaly-detection methods. Finally, we list two possible approaches to developing a model capable of searching for these surface technosignatures: a supervised and an unsupervised one. Complemented by LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, and reflectance spectroscopy, these methods would enable the first quantitative upper limits on surface technosignatures while yielding ancillary benefits for planetary science.

papers.title: Data-driven characterisation of variable source light curves with multimodal representation learning
papers.abstract: Surveys such as the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) produce light curves for hundreds of millions of variables. Their characterisation traditionally relies on supervised classifiers with hand-crafted features and curated labels, limiting them to predefined taxonomies and individual surveys. We present a general, survey-agnostic framework that characterises variable sources without labelled training data, producing low-dimensional representations of light curve properties such as amplitude, periodicity, and asymmetry. A multimodal architecture combines two complementary views, a Transformer encoder on raw observations and a convolutional neural network on a generalised Lomb-Scargle periodogram. Each light curve is randomly split into two temporal halves as independent views, and the branches are trained jointly with VICReg to produce embeddings invariant across halves while keeping each dimension informative. We evaluate on 37 006 ZTF sources spanning 14 variable star classes in four broad physical categories. A linear classifier on the frozen 64-dimensional embeddings achieves 77.1% balanced accuracy for classes and 90.5% for broad categories. Combining both branches improves balanced accuracy by up to 14.9 percentage points over the best single modality, confirming their complementarity. Interpretable light curve properties are encoded on distinct dimensions, and within-class analysis reveals physical substructure unresolved by reference labels. Retraining on ZTF g and i bands without modification reproduces the main results, and concatenating multi-band embeddings improves balanced accuracy to 86.1%. The framework needs no labels, phase folding, or survey-specific preprocessing and applies directly to other surveys with different cadences and wavelength coverage.

papers.title: A design concept for the High Resolution Imager on the Habitable Worlds Observatory
papers.abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will be NASA's next flagship astrophysics mission, designed to search for signs of life on planets around nearby stars and conduct transformational science across astrophysics. Its High Resolution Imager (HRI) is not only the observatory's main imaging camera, but also provides grism spectroscopy and sub-microarcsecond astrometry, as well as the observatory's fine guidance, wavefront sensing and pupil imaging. We present a design concept for HRI, developed during concurrent design sessions by flowing down science requirements within the envelope of NASA's EAC-1 telescope architecture. Light from a 3'x2' field is collimated by two mirrors, then divided by a dichroic for simultaneous observations in an ultraviolet-to-visible arm covering 200-900 nm and a near-infrared arm covering 0.9-2.2 um. By minimising the number of reflective surfaces upstream of the dichroic, our optical design maximises throughput and stability, while reducing wavefront error. Readout modes can be chosen in orbit to image the entire field in exposures of at least 10 seconds, or in smaller windows for observations up to 1 kHz. Throughout, we emphasise the interplay between subsystems that couple design choices.

papers.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science
papers.abstract: The Pandora spacecraft is a smallsat selected in NASA's inaugural class of Pioneers missions. The aim of the Pandora mission is to disentangle stellar activity signals from exoplanet atmospheric transmission spectroscopy measurements. Pandora accomplishes this goal with its combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy that observe each target in the prime mission for 10 separate transit observations, each spanning 24 hours at a time. Targets were carefully selected for the Pandora prime mission. Pandora is specifically studying planets around low-mass stellar hosts (K and M dwarf stars) spanning a range of rotation periods and activity levels. The planets range in size from 1.5 - 15 Earth radii and orbital periods ranging from 1.7 - 11.5 days. In addition to the 10 transit visits planned for each of the 20 prime mission targets, Pandora is observing a number of auxiliary targets encompassing a variety of science topics. This includes topics such as stellar activity and young systems, transit timing variations of exoplanets, brown dwarf compositions, exoplanet phase curves, etc. We will discuss the selection of these targets, how they have been scheduled to fill in gaps in prime mission operations, and early science results. If the mission is extended, there is further opportunity for accomplishing additional science. Here we will discuss the possible options for extended mission operations and science.

papers.title: Rotation in the Lagoon Nebula with K2
papers.abstract: A low-mass star's rotation rate drives its magnetic field, and in the case of young stars, also affects accretion and planetary formation. Observations of the rotation rates of young stars help constrain models of star and planet formation. We present rotation rates from K2 observations of stars in the ~1-2 Myr Lagoon Nebula, one of the youngest clusters with space-based rotation rates available. From 414 light curves we obtain reliable rotation periods for 325 stars; 124 of them are disk-bearing and 201 are disk-free. This constitutes a significant increase in the collection of K2 rotation rates available for ~1-5 Myr stars. The overall distribution is broadly consistent with expectations, in that the slowest rotators are mid-K and both lower and higher masses are on average faster rotating. There is weak evidence that disked stars rotate more slowly. There are a few complex periodic variables, but they appear to be surprisingly high mass compared to prior known examples of this kind of object.

papers.title: Coronal spectroscopy - Past, Present and Future
papers.abstract: After the beginning of photography of solar corona during the eclipses in the year 1860, efforts began to carry out spectroscopic observations of solar corona. During the total solar eclipse of 1868 August 18 at Guntur, Madras state, the observation of emission line 5875{\AA} by Janssen lead to the discovery of Helium. Next year, during the eclipse of 1869 August 7, Charles Young and William Harkness discovered green emission line around 5310{\AA} (later measured as 5303{\AA}). It was interpreted as due to Coronium, an unknown element. The identification of this green line in 1939 due to [Fe xiv] ion showed the corona to be hot at 10^6 K. High resolution spectroscopic observations indicated that width of emission lines to be more than expected. The excess line width was interpreted in terms of existence of non-thermal velocity. Recent spectroscopic observations have indicated a complex nature of variation of emission line parameters with height above the corona. The spectroscopy of solar corona is also performed in other wavelengths, such as UV, EUV, X-rays, visible, infrared, and radio part of the spectrum. Here, we discuss the past spectroscopic observations of solar corona, present observations with various instruments, such as Visible Emission Line Coronagraph onboard Aditya-L1, and need for the spectroscopic observations in future.

papers.title: Relation of Rotation and Pulsation Properties in $\gamma$ Doradus Stars
papers.abstract: Connection between stellar rotation and pulsation amplitude has been proposed for several types of pulsating variable stars, but no such relation has been established for gamma Doradus stars from spectroscopic v sin i measurements. A high-amplitude gamma Dor subclass was also suggested recently, which had not been explored by spectroscopic means before. We investigate the connection between rotation and pulsational properties of gamma Dor stars using a homogeneous spectroscopic sample with available TESS light curves. We obtained new stellar spectra with the ACE spectrograph on the 1-m RCC telescope of Konkoly Observatory and measured v sin i for a sample of 124 targets. For target selection, Gaia classifications were combined with TESS photometry. We used Fourier methods to determine the dominant frequencies from all available TESS light curves through sector 98. We also performed rotation- and inclination-dependent mode visibility modelling relying on GYRE Hough functions with TAR visibilities for the interpretation of our results. We find a decreasing upper envelope in both the peak-to-peak amplitude and the dominant-component semi-amplitude as a function of v sin i: high-v sin i stars show only low photometric amplitudes, whereas high-amplitude stars have low v sin i. We also confirm a positive relation between v sin i and the dominant pulsation frequency. The highest observed amplitudes also decrease towards higher dominant frequencies. Visibility modelling indicates that these trends cannot be explained by geometric effects alone, suggesting that the intrinsic pulsation amplitudes of gamma Dor stars physically decrease with increasing equatorial rotational velocity. Furthermore, the strong suppression of zonal dipole mode visibility at high rotation suggests that high-amplitude gamma Dor stars are likely slow rotators or moderate rotators viewed nearly pole-on.

papers.title: OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584: Discovery of a gas giant orbiting an M dwarf
papers.abstract: We report the discovery and characterization of a planetary system in the microlensing event OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584. We analyze photometric data from OGLE and MOA surveys, as well as LCO, $\mu$FUN, and Mindstep follow-up telescopes to model the microlensing light curve. We also used data from the Keck II telescope collected in 2018 to obtain additional constraints on the lensing system. We found a Saturn-mass planet of mass $M_{\rm p}=105\pm13 \ M_\oplus$ orbiting a low-mass host star $M_{\rm L}=0.139\pm0.011 \ M_\odot$ at $1.00\pm0.08$ kpc from Earth. This discovery adds to the small sample of giant planets orbiting low-mass stars and provides constraints on planet formation theories.

papers.title: SpinOctopus: A Versatile, User-Friendly, and Extensible Public Code for General-Relativistic Ray-Tracing in axisymmetric spacetime
papers.abstract: Relativistic ray-tracing algorithms serve as indispensable numerical tools for investigating gravitational theories and high-energy astrophysics. In this paper, we develop and release SpinOctopus, a versatile relativistic ray-tracing code tailored for arbitrary axisymmetric spacetimes, powered by a Fortran/Python hybrid architecture and OpenMP multi-threading acceleration. This numerical toolkit is capable of simulating timelike orbits and their corresponding light curves, null geodesics, as well as black hole images illuminated by a wide array of phenomenological sources, including geometrically thin and thick accretion disks, geometrically thin tilted disks, relativistic jets, spherically symmetric accretion flows, and point sources. To execute these tasks, users are solely required to specify the covariant metric tensor of the target spacetime and the simulation parameters within a dedicated configuration file. Benefiting from our customized adaptive step-size strategy for geodesic integration, SpinOctopus achieves an impressive processing efficiency of $\sim 800$ rays per second per thread on an Intel Core i7-14700 platform when simulating geometrically thick accretion disk images. Furthermore, the code provides transparent interfaces, allowing users to seamlessly modify the geometric and kinematic properties of the light sources. Additional capabilities, such as simulating Fe K${\alpha}$ fluorescent line profiles and geometrically thick tilted accretion disk images, will be introduced in future releases of the framework.

papers.title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
papers.abstract: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear G\"udel-Benz relation.

papers.title: Optimization of Petal-Shaped Occulters for Exo-Earth Observation
papers.abstract: Petal-shaped occulters are giant, formation-flying optical devices designed for use in space astronomy. Their primary function is to block the intense starlight to enable the direct observation of exoplanets, a process challenged by the extreme contrast ratio (lower than 1e-10 for an exo-Earth). This study focuses on optimizing the shape of the occulter in order to significantly reduce Fresnel diffraction. For a circular occulter, the diffraction pattern shows the bright Arago spot. Nevertheless, we construct an apodized occulter as the weighted sum of circular occulters of various diameters, owing to the fact that their diffraction are complex amplitudes which can, with adequate weighting, interfere with each other in such a way as to form a resulting diffraction pattern with a very dark central area. This basis of circular occulters allows the use of a simple analytical form for their Fresnel diffraction. First, occulter diameters are fixed on a regularly sampled linear scale, and the weights are obtained by minimizing a quadratic criterion. An improvement is then obtained using a combined optimization over the weights and the diameters sizes. Eventually, the apodized profile is used to design the petal-shaped occulter for physical imple- mentation constraints. The resulting rejection rates are comparable to the results obtained using SISTER ( http://sister.caltech.edu ), which uses a completely different non-parametric approach.

papers.title: In search of the third dimension in Compton X-ray polarimeters
papers.abstract: Compton polarimeters are typically designed to be sensitive only to the azimuthal angle of the scattered photon, ignoring the scattering angle. Such a 2-dimensional reconstruction of the event is pursued for both simplicity and because the polarization of the incident photon influences only the azimuthal response of the instrument. While this is true for on-axis sources, when the source starts to be off-axis of several degrees the azimuthal response of the instrument is effectively a convolution of the azimuthal and polar scattering angles: measuring the latter would provide a better sensitivity and smaller systematic effects. In this contribution, we will present a design which allows to estimate the scattering angle in a Compton polarimeter through the read-out of the light signal at the two ends of scintillator bars. Such a design is being tested with a representative set-up and first results on the performance are presented.

papers.title: In-orbit anomaly and recovery of IXPE detector 2
papers.abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) is a joint NASA-ASI mission launched in December 2021 to measure the linear polarization of celestial X-ray sources in the 2-8 keV energy range. The payload comprises three identical telescopes, each combining grazing-incidence X-ray optics with a focal-plane photoelectric polarimeter based on the Gas Pixel Detector technology. On 14 April 2025, the second detector experienced an anomaly that significantly altered the electrical behavior of the ASIC responsible for reading out the photoelectron track images. In this contribution, we describe the effect of the anomaly on the instrumental response and the actions taken to mitigate its effects and recover the scientific observations of the instrument.

papers.title: Cosmic Ray Observations using Coincident Scintillator and Radio Signals with the Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON)
papers.abstract: At energies above 100 PeV, coherent radio frequency (RF) emission across the 10 -- 1000 MHz band from cosmic particle-induced atmospheric showers becomes increasingly dominant, making radio detection a powerful probe at ultrahigh energies. The Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON) considers mountaintop phased radio arrays to monitor large areas at the horizon for upward-going geomagnetic emission in the 30 -- 80 MHz band produced as a consequence of Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. As part of ongoing efforts to measure the sensitivity of BEACON to such signals, the BEACON prototype identifies cosmic rays through the same emission mechanism. Prior to 2023, BEACON operated a four-antenna prototype, which successfully demonstrated identification of coherent and impulsive sources using a beamforming RF trigger. In 2023, we upgraded the instrument to six newly designed antennas and added an independent scintillator array to cross-validate radio-detectable cosmic rays. This work details the observation of 22 candidate cosmic-ray events in a scintillator-coincidence-triggered dataset using selection cuts based on expected radio characteristics. A simulation of the hybrid-instrument performance verifies this observation rate to within an order of magnitude. We estimate a background of 0.11 events by applying the selection cuts to synthetic datasets of uncorrelated radio-scintillator pairs that are randomly formed using fixed-rate software-triggered data. The reconstructed signal polarization angles are consistent with pure geomagnetic emission compared to various background classes.

papers.title: Direct Injection of Chemically-Enhanced Plasma into a Solar Flare Arcade
papers.abstract: The magnetic reconnection event that drives "standard" solar flares ejects material from the reconnection site, loading mass directly onto the newly-reconnected flare arcade. To et al (2024) suggested that this model can explain observations of the distribution of elemental abundances measured in post-flare loops: the reconnection exhaust directly injects plasma with coronal abundances onto the arcade, flowing from the apex downwards. We test this idea directly by modeling the spatiotemporal variation of elements with low first ionization potential (FIP), and directly inject material near loop apices. We show that this direct injection is capable of producing enhancements similar in magnitude and spatial spread across the corona to those observed during the gradual phase of an X11.9 flare. We also show that direct chromospheric heating strongly limits the width of the low-FIP enhancement to a narrow region near the injection site. The enhancement of low-FIP elemental abundances naturally explains bright knots commonly observed near the top of flare arcades.

papers.title: Enhanced Mass Transfer from Extended Shock-Supported Stellar Chromospheres
papers.abstract: Mass transfer (MT) in binary systems is a crucial and complex process. Even before the donor's photosphere fills its Roche lobe, matter from its outer atmosphere can reach the inner Lagrange point, thus initiating interaction in the so-called optically thin phase. Most existing models account for a very tenuous atmosphere supported by thermal gas pressure, thus predicting very little MT until the donor fills its Roche lobe. However, recent hydrodynamic simulations of giant stars suggest that shock-driven outflows can create substantially thicker "chromospheres'' extending to a few stellar radii. In this work, we derive a simple analytic model for a shock-supported chromosphere in a binary potential and calculate the corresponding MT rate. We also implement our prescription in the stellar evolution code MESA. We show that chromospheric MT rates can be orders of magnitude higher than prior estimates for optically thin MT, especially for stars high on the red giant or asymptotic giant branch. This allows for substantial accretion before Roche lobe overflow, both for systems that undergo stable mass transfer and for systems that go through common envelope evolution. Thus, for a given initial binary configuration, this may alter the final period and component masses compared to those predicted classically. Our model is similar to Wind Roche-lobe Overflow, but it is physically rather than empirically motivated. We discuss implications for various post-interaction binaries that can be tested with population synthesis studies and observed binary populations. Additionally, we have identified an inaccuracy in the current implementation of the optically-thin Ritter 1988 prescription in MESA, which we correct.

papers.title: Stellar Loci X: Selection of Nitrogen-Rich Giants Using GALEX NUV and Synthetic SDSS Photometry
papers.abstract: Nitrogen-rich (N-rich) field stars (likely second-generation escapees from globular clusters) provide a powerful, but currently sample-limited, probe of globular-cluster disruption in the Galactic halo. We exploit the fact that enhanced NH, CN absorption depresses optical u band flux, while the near-ultraviolet (NUV) band is largely insensitive to nitrogen enhancement while remaining sensitive to overall metallicity. Combining GALEX NUV photometry with (synthetic) SDSS optical photometry, we construct a [Fe/H]-dependent stellar-locus model for giants and select significant redder u-g outliers as N-rich candidates. For a relaxed cut ([Fe/H] <= -0.8, 2 sigma) we identify 970 candidates, with an estimated completeness of 64-65% and purity of 41-62% from multiple validations. A stricter selection ([Fe/H] <= -1.0, 3 sigma) yields 220 candidates, with lower completeness (30-38%) but substantially higher purity (60-91%). The dominant contaminants show anomalous spectral energy distributions (e.g., UV excess), and are themselves useful targets for follow-up. The diverse kinematic and dynamical properties of our candidates suggest multiple origins. This scalable photometric approach enables systematic searches for N-rich halo stars and is well suited to forthcoming wide-field surveys such as CSST.

papers.title: Neutron Star-Main-Sequence Star Collision: Formation and Long-Term Evolution of Thorne-\.Zytkow Objects
papers.abstract: Thorne-$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$ytkow objects (T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$Os) are stars containing a neutron-star (NS) or black-hole (BH) core embedded in a stellar envelope and powered primarily by mass accretion onto the core. Classical evolution models of T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$Os begin with an assumed equilibrium configuration and predict chemical anomalies in the stellar envelope resulting from nuclear burning in the vicinity of the NS core. Here we connect dynamical formation to long-term evolution by combining a three-dimensional simulation of a post-supernova collision between a $1.4M_\odot$ NS and a $10M_\odot$ main-sequence star with a subsequent stellar evolution calculation using MESA. The collision successfully produces a bound, quasi-spherical T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$O with the NS settled at the center of the stellar envelope. In contrast to the classical picture, the collision heats a substantial fraction of the star and leads to widespread nuclear burning during the subsequent thermal-relaxation phase. As the envelope becomes convective, material processed by the carbon-nitrogen cycle is transported to the surface, leaving a potentially observable chemical imprint of formation that persists after the star attains the standard accretion-supported T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$O structure. At the end of our simulation, the stellar luminosity greatly exceeds Eddington in the outer envelope, suggesting that significant mass ejection will occur, leaving behind an isolated NS or BH.

papers.title: The diversity of late-time interaction in Type II supernovae
papers.abstract: Studying core-collapse supernovae (SNe) beyond one year after explosion, when ejecta interaction with circumstellar material (CSM) progressively becomes the dominant power source, offers critical insights into the progenitor mass loss history. Using binary progenitors that underwent different levels of H-rich envelope stripping, we present radiative transfer calculations of the ejecta with CSM interaction in Type IIb, II-L and II-P SN scenarios covering epochs of 1.5 to 3-6yr, with a focus on the UV and optical properties. The impact of CSM interaction is evaluated for a cold-dense shell (CDS) of 0.1-2.0Msun (CDS velocity of ~5000-10000km/s) and shock powers of 1e39-1e41erg/s, producing a grid of about 200 models. We find that Lyalpha, MgII2800, and Halpha are typically the strongest individual lines, MgII2800 being the most constant relative to changes in time and in CDS mass. Lyalpha thrives at low CDS mass and is strongly attenuated otherwise. A large fraction of the emerging UV and optical flux is, however, influenced by a forest of Fe lines, which introduces strong optical depth effects. A myriad of other lines, generally forbidden, are predicted that each contain less than a percent of the total flux. N enrichment yield stronger N lines in the UV and optical. A subset of these models roughly match UV and optical observations of SNe 1993J, 1998S, 2013ej, and 2023ixf at 1.5-3yr, although matching the full range consistently is a challenge, in particular when dust must be invoked. Blue-red asymmetry of line profiles is typical of all lines in the UV, the more so at earlier times or higher CDS mass, even in the absence of dust. In our simulations, optical depth effects, associated with the gas or dust or both, quenches the emission of Lyalpha or [OIII]4958-5007A from regions within or below the CDS.

papers.title: Surface regolith model of near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon
papers.abstract: The near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon displays activity as it comes close to the Sun and is presumed to be the progenitor of the Geminids meteor shower. Both CM- and CY-meteorites have been suggested as possible meteorite analogues for Phaethon. Previous spectral and polarization measurements of Phaethon indicate possible surface heterogeneity in the regolith properties. By combining mineral components and their size fractions, we present a regolith model for Phaethon that reproduces the spectral, polarization, and geometric albedo measurements presented in various studies, with the aim of quantitatively characterizing the surface material and structure, as well as the regolith heterogeneity. The best fit model able to produce the measurements is constructed from large olivine particles with troilite inclusions and small scale surface roughness, mixed with smaller, porous troilite aggregates comprised of monomers resembling interplanetary dust. Our model suggests that the different spectral and polarization responses of the regolith are caused by changes in the size and amount of the small dark troilite particles. Based on the amount of troilite in the regolith model, we propose that CM-meteorites are the preferable meteorite analogue for Phaethon.

papers.title: The morphology of contact binary objects in the Solar System
papers.abstract: Contact binaries, appearing as two objects stuck together, are prevalent throughout the Solar System, making up between 30- 50% of asteroids and comets. Despite this, detailed shape models of contact binaries are hard to obtain remotely, requiring rare occultation events or close approaches to Earth (< 0.1 au) to observe with ground-based radar systems. Despite only 16 contact binary models being published, there already exists a wide variety of different arrangements of the two lobes relative to one another. At the same time, simulations of contact binary object formation are increasing in scale, producing 10s to 1000s of contact binary candidates per simulation. It is therefore necessary to begin the process of characterising the different shapes observed, and to further investigate any emerging trends. We analyse the size, period, neck prominence, volume distribution, ratio between the sizes and volumes of the individual lobes, and the alignment between them to summarise the extent of the currently modelled asteroids.

papers.title: Topographically Forced Stationary Waves Can Explain the Near-Surface Zonal Winds Observed by Huygens on Titan
papers.abstract: Titan's equatorial superrotation is associated with climatological retrograde (westward) near-surface winds at low latitudes, as consistently simulated by Titan general circulation models. However, the Huygens probe measured prograde (eastward) near-surface winds, contrary to the expected circulation. We investigate whether these observations reflect localized forcing by large-scale topography, using paired three-dimensional dry simulations with and without topography in the Titan Atmospheric Model. We find that topography generates longitude-locked, vertically structured zonal wind anomalies that reproduce key features of the Huygens wind profile in the lowest few kilometers. Helmholtz and spectral analyses show that this structure arises from the superposition of several vertically varying low wavenumber modes. A predominantly rotational, topographically forced stationary zonal wavenumber s=1 response provides a major eastward anomaly throughout the lowest 2 km, whereas a locally divergent s=4 response consistent with a gravity wave, opposes it near the surface. Weaker s=2 and s=3 responses also vary vertically and contribute eastward anomalies near the surface. Combined with the retrograde zonal-mean circulation, these modes produce a Huygens-like profile characterized by prograde flow within the lowest 1 km and shear toward retrograde flow aloft. The paired simulations establish their topographic origin, while coherence with the corresponding terrain-forcing components demonstrates that the responses remain phase locked to the forcing. Similar but weaker stationary responses are simulated near the planned Dragonfly landing site, providing baseline expectations for interpreting its future atmospheric measurements. This study demonstrates how large-scale topography can generate localized departures from Titan's zonal-mean circulation and highlights the importance of stationary waves.

papers.title: Predictions for an unseen third planet in the WISPIT 2 system
papers.abstract: We predict the mass and semi-major axis of a currently unseen but hypothesised planet in the WISPIT 2 system based on the location of the ring observed by ALMA at 144.4 au. Using findings from previous hydrodynamical models, we predict that a ~0.2-1 $M_{Jup}$ planet may exist at ~ 100-120 au. We also demonstrate that the ring seen in VLT/SPHERE observations at 96.7 au is consistent with the mass and semi-major axis of WISPIT 2b and confirm that WISPIT 2b cannot be the cause of the ALMA ring. We also discuss how future observations of the system's gas component may help constrain these predictions better, and note that this third planet in WISPIT 2 may be discoverable using upcoming JWST/NIRCam observations or Gaia data release 4 (DR4).

papers.title: Noisy Pipelines I: An end-to-end pipeline to perform multivariate noise inference for LISA
papers.abstract: Instrumental data from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) must be post-processed prior to any global-fit based analysis. For example, it is critical to filter, downsample, segment and window the data in order to perform inference of both the signal and noise parameters in the frequency domain. Each step alters the noise process, requiring a correction to the noise covariance matrix that describes the underlying data stream. We present $\texttt{lisa-noise}$, a JAX-based noise inference pipeline that returns a spectral estimate of the noise process subject to post-processing effects. We fit splines to the underlying secondary noises and fit the full multivariate $3 \times 3$ covariance matrix of the Michelson channels. We assume unequal and non-constant arm-lengths throughout. The drift of the zeros of the transfer functions, a non-stationary effect, is captured by averaging the transfer functions over a number of epochs within each segment. On 30 days of conditioned simulated data, a likelihood evaluation costs $3\,$ms on a current laptop for a 7 day segment. A gradient-based fit from a tight prior recovers the injected spectra in a fraction of a second. A multi-start search over large priors $\pm 10$ in $\log_{10}$ centred on the simulated truth obtains a noise estimate consistent with the data, verified by Bayesian techniques. The fitted covariance whitens the conditioned data in every band and through every zero of the transfer functions, in a form that global-fit pipelines can use directly.

papers.title: Arepo-CD: Coupling Collisional $N$-Body Dynamics with Moving-Mesh Magnetohydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Star formation is a hierarchical, clustered process in turbulent giant molecular clouds (GMCs), where close stellar encounters can strongly affect cluster evolution and feedback. However, gravitational softening in many hydrodynamic simulations of GMCs limits the treatment of these encounters. We present Arepo-CD (Collisional Dynamics), a framework that couples star-by-star collisional $N$-body dynamics to the moving-mesh magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code Arepo. Star-star interactions use unsoftened gravity, while interactions involving gas or collisionless components remain softened. Compact stellar subsystems are identified on the fly and evolved with a fourth-order forward symplectic integrator and slow-down algorithmic regularization coupled to the native Arepo timestep hierarchy. Benchmark tests against the collisional $N$-body code PeTar show good agreement in cluster core collapse and subsequent expansion, radial density profiles, and stellar velocity distributions. Coupled to the Rigel star formation and feedback model, Arepo-CD follows cluster formation and early evolution in radiation MHD simulations of a $10^5~M_\odot$ turbulent molecular cloud. In the fiducial GMC comparison, the collisional and softened-gravity runs yield similar star formation histories and integrated star formation efficiencies. Nevertheless, close gravitational encounters during the embedded phase generate a substantial runaway population, with a velocity tail extending beyond 100 km/s. Ejected massive stars redistribute radiative feedback into the surrounding lower-density medium and produce a more extended distribution of heated gas. Arepo-CD provides a practical and computationally efficient framework for studying collisional stellar dynamics and its coupling to gas evolution and feedback during star cluster formation in realistic galactic environments.

papers.title: Prior volume effect inflates the gravitational-wave background in pulsar timing arrays
papers.abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) have found evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background (GWB) whose amplitude exceeds most predictions based on supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs). Using NANOGrav 15-year data, we show that a substantial part of this excess arises from a prior volume effect. The GWB amplitude is constrained mainly by the pulsars' auto-correlations, where the GWB is degenerate with each pulsar's intrinsic red noise. By decomposing the GWB posterior, we find that marginalizing over the standard log-uniform red-noise priors introduces a prior volume term that favors a stronger GWB, pulling the inferred amplitude more than $2\sigma$ above the maximum-likelihood estimate. The Hellings-Downs (HD) cross-correlations, which measure the GWB alone, are not strong enough to counter the volume term. The profile likelihood, a cross-correlation-only estimator, and priors that are uniform in power or informed by the pulsar population all avoid or reduce this effect and lower the amplitude into agreement with SMBHBs. The revised priors also yield a steeper GWB spectrum closer to the SMBHB predictions, strengthen the evidence for HD correlations, and weaken the preference for new-physics sources over SMBHBs.

papers.title: Systematic Uncertainties in Rocky Exoplanet Reflected Light from Incomplete Laboratory BRDF Measurements
papers.abstract: The first observations of short-period rocky exoplanets have initiated the era of terrestrial exoplanet characterization. The interpretation of these observations relies on forward models used in atmospheric and surface retrieval frameworks. While atmospheric modeling is supported by extensive laboratory datasets of molecular opacities, the experimental basis for rocky surface characterization remains limited. Most reflectance libraries of planetary analog materials provide spectra measured at a single illumination and viewing geometry, constraining the spectral behavior but not its full angular scattering properties. We show that incomplete angular coverage in laboratory bidirectional reflectance measurements introduces an intrinsic systematic uncertainty in the interpretation of rocky exoplanet observations. We demonstrate that multiple combinations of photometric parameters can reproduce the same laboratory reflectance spectrum while predicting different angular scattering behaviors and disk-integrated observables. We propagate this non-uniqueness to reflected-light phase curves, geometric albedos, and planet-star contrast ratios between $0.5$--$1.7\,\mu$m, representative of the spectral range targeted by future direct-imaging missions such as the HWO. We find that single-geometry laboratory spectra produce large uncertainties in predicted signals, particularly at small phase angles. Simplified assumptions adopted in exoplanet studies, such as isotropic scattering can additionally introduce systematic biases. Using multi-angular laboratory measurements from the Bloomsburg University Goniometer dataset, we show that the uncertainty in predicted observables collapses once angular scattering behavior is directly constrained. Our results demonstrate that multi-angular measurements are required to construct physically predictive reflected-light models of rocky exoplanets.

papers.title: PIANISTpy: A JAX-based Python package for velocity-anisotropic astrophysical equilibrium models
papers.abstract: The hierarchical assembly of dark matter haloes and galaxies via mergers and anisotropic mass accretion naturally imprints non-trivial velocity anisotropy onto haloes and galaxies, an empirical fact emerging from cosmological simulations. However, dynamical studies based on idealised numerical simulations typically assume isotropic velocity distributions for the systems studied. This is mainly because no tools exist to construct anisotropic initial conditions with fully self-consistent (i.e., physical and instability-free) truncation boundary conditions for finite spatial extents. Here we present the first such analytical framework that performs truncation in phase space, with two distinct approaches to guarantee either the monotonicity of output distribution functions or identical truncated density profiles. We additionally present the open-source JAX-based GPU-accelerated Python package PIANISTpy (Particle Initial conditions with ANISoTropy) for constructing spherical, non-rotating initial conditions, supporting arbitrary double-power-law analytical radial density profiles and a library of analytical anisotropy profiles. This framework further permits the construction of systems with non-analytical anisotropy profiles via an arbitrary linear superposition of all implemented analytical anisotropy models as basis functions. PIANISTpy also outputs 3D velocity profiles and line-of-sight-integrated observables with end-to-end differentiability for rapid gradient-based Monte Carlo inference, and self-consistent local dark matter velocity distributions of anisotropic haloes beyond the unphysical Maxwell-Boltzmann simplification adopted in terrestrial detection experiments. We discuss use cases and demonstrate PIANISTpy's orders-of-magnitude higher numerical solver accuracy and superior dynamical stability of particle initial conditions relative to existing tools, including galpy and AGAMA.

papers.title: KROME-X: a GPU-ready library for chemistry and microphysics in astrophysical simulations
papers.abstract: KROME is a Python pre-processor that writes a complete Fortran solver of chemistry and microphysics for each chemical network, widely used in astrophysical simulations. We introduce here KROME-X, a complete rewrite of KROME in modern C++, which incorporates updated physics. A code generator translates a declarative network description into a compact core (rates, right-hand side, analytic Jacobian, thermal terms, and tables), which a fixed, header-only runtime integrates with a C++ port of the `backward differentiation formula' method of CVODE (SUNDIALS). The physics is validated against legacy KROME and independent references. On the legacy test cases KROME-X reproduces legacy KROME to the accuracy of the solvers, wherever the physics is the same, and is up to 13.5 times faster at equal tolerance. On NVIDIA A100 GPUs, it can outperform its share of a computing node from a few thousand cells per call, with the highest throughput (5 to 30) obtained for $10^5$ cells per batch. Networks of hundreds of species still run faster on the CPU due to the GPU's limited memory capacity. The new version also includes, among other changes, on-the-fly co-evolution of a photon field alongside chemistry, which conserves photons exactly; the secondary ionizations using the photoelectron energy of each absorption; dust evolution in size and temperature with a true grain energy equation; line cooling rates rebuilt from current atomic and molecular data, and incorporating optical thickness effects. KROME-X therefore represents the natural successor of KROME and provides a portable, extensible framework for astrochemical kinetics on both CPUs and GPUs for future hydrodynamic simulations.

papers.title: Dual-Phase Flow Matching for Probabilistic Source Detection and Measurement in Astronomical Images
papers.abstract: Using the largest digital camera ever built, the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will image over half the night sky. Most astronomical analyses of LSST data operate not on images but on catalogs derived from them: tables of light sources detailing their positions, fluxes (colors and brightnesses), and types (e.g., star, galaxy). At LSST's imaging depths, light sources often overlap visually, so the configuration of sources in each image is itself uncertain. Nevertheless, LSST's cataloging pipeline commits to a single source configuration, which can bias downstream analyses. Here, we instead approximate a posterior distribution over source configurations. Our posterior approximation is a continuous-time Markov process (CTMP) fitted by generator matching, an extension of flow matching to non-Euclidean state spaces. This CTMP generates a source configuration in two phases: it detects light sources in the first and measures them in the second. On simulated LSST-like data, the proposed method produces better posterior approximations than five comparison methods: two Markov chain Monte Carlo methods that run thousands of times more slowly at survey scales; two neural posterior estimation methods; and one ablation of the proposed method that lacks the dual-phase structure. Applied to LSST Data Preview 1 (DP1), the first public release of Rubin imaging, the proposed method alone recovers small-scale galaxy clustering in agreement with higher-resolution Hubble imaging and reports uncertainty that remains calibrated against that reference as blending increases. We deliver a probabilistic catalog of the Extended Chandra Deep Field South region, one of the most extensively studied extragalactic fields, and use it to characterize the galaxy color-magnitude distribution.

papers.title: How general relativity stacks up: Testing gravity by coherently combining gravitational-wave observations
papers.abstract: A core mission of gravitational-wave astronomy is to test general relativity (GR) in the high-curvature, high-velocity regime. The field has already seen significant progress in this space, though a remaining challenge is how to combine data from a population of binary mergers. This can both boost the significance of potential GR violations, and develop a phenomenological picture of how deviations manifest in different mergers. We propose a framework to coherently combine gravitational-wave measurements to build a population-level test of physics beyond GR. We assume that deviations from GR are (i) strongest near the merger, (ii) vary smoothly with the total mass of the binary, and (iii) are most prominent in the $\ell=|m|=2$ mode. While these assumptions do not describe every possible deviation of GR, they provide us with a plausible starting point upon which a more general framework can be built. We apply our framework to 28 high signal-to-noise ratio binary black hole mergers from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's Fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog, finding no evidence for deviations from GR. Our framework allows one to show how deviations could vary as a function of total mass of the system. We argue that such a reconstruction can be used to convincingly distinguish between systematic waveform errors and genuine GR violations.

papers.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Technical Foundations for Quantitative 450/850 $\mu$m JCMT SCUBA-2/POL-2 Polarimetry
papers.abstract: We present five technical validations of SCUBA-2/POL-2 polarimetry on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at 450 and 850 $\mu$m, using 174 archival fields in 69 molecular cloud regions and subsets appropriate to each test. Extended-source calibration avoids a deterministic shift of $\Delta\beta=-1.05$ in the dust emissivity index $\beta$ that would result from calibrating extended emission using peak brightness. We modeled Stokes $I$ noise with additive and signal-dependent components. The measured median ratio of surface-brightness noise at 450/850 $\mu$m is 25. Independent tests of Stokes $Q,U$ noise support approximately equal additive variances and weak error correlations, providing a basis for propagating polarization uncertainties. Corrections determined for individual fields reduce additive zero-level offsets of order $1$ mJy arcsec$^{-2}$ in the 450 $\mu$m Stokes $Q$ and $U$ intensities. The three-step regression leaves a median combined residual amplitude of $0.07$ mJy arcsec$^{-2}$. Independent comparisons with SOFIA/HAWC+ at 154 and 214 $\mu$m support the correction in strongly affected fields. We matched the 450 $\mu$m maps to the modeled 850 $\mu$m beam and the common $12.6''$-$300''$ range of angular scales. We compared three reductions of the same 450 $\mu$m observations across 30 sources. Taking the median angular residual relative to the final product for each source, we find that beam matching reduces the median over sources from $6.3^\circ$ to $4.7^\circ$. After matching, 29 of the 30 sources have median residuals below $10^\circ$. We also quantified how residual $Q/U$ offsets propagate in ratios of polarization fractions, differences in spectral indices, and polarization angles. These validations provide procedures and quantitative references for interpreting POL-2 measurements and combining them with polarimetry at other wavelengths.

papers.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Dual-Wavelength Constraints on Size-Dependent Grain Alignment in Star-Forming Regions
papers.abstract: We compared 450 and 850 $\mu$m POL-2 observations from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at $12.6''$ resolution. The median absolute difference in polarization angle between bands is $6.7^\circ$ across 21 regions. For total intensity $I\propto\nu^\alpha$ and polarized intensity $PI\propto\nu^\gamma$, 24-27 of 35 regions have $\gamma<\alpha$, allowing for $3\sigma$ limits on weak polarized intensities. The median $\gamma-\alpha$ is $-0.51$, ranging from $-0.57$ to $-0.45$ under these limits. The ratio of polarization fractions is $P_{450}/P_{850}=0.69\pm0.02_{\rm sys}\pm0.03_{\rm stat}$, with no detected dependence on the angle difference. We suggest that the dependence of alignment on grain size offers the simplest explanation of these findings. For optically thin components sharing a polarization angle and opacity law, temperature mixing reproduces the median $-0.51$ only if the warm dust is polarized less efficiently than the cold dust. If the cold dust is at 10 K or warmer and the warm dust at 40 K or cooler, the median requires a ratio of warm to cold effective polarization efficiencies $r\lesssim0.18$. We tested mixtures with opacity index $\beta=2$ in four fields against Herschel dust temperatures and Green Bank Ammonia Survey kinetic temperatures. We assumed equal gas and dust temperatures, ammonia tracing cold gas, and model ranges of 3-20 K for cold dust and 25-40 K for warm dust carrying at most half the mass. Mixtures matching both temperatures cannot reproduce $\gamma-\alpha$ within $1\sigma$ in three fields, including OMC 2 tentatively, even for $r=0$. Allowing warm dust at 10-100 K and up to 95% of the mass permits solutions only for $r\leq0.041$. To explain these three fields by temperature mixing, we need wider model ranges and a very strong contrast in polarization efficiency. The origin of this contrast remains undetermined.

papers.title: simesh: A Python Framework for Quantitative Analysis of Native AMR Data from MPI-AMRVAC
papers.abstract: Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) is widely used in large-scale astrophysical simulations, but the resulting multilevel data are challenging to analyze quantitatively. We present simesh, an independent Python framework for quantitative analysis of cell-centered fields on block-structured AMR meshes. The current implementation targets three-dimensional Cartesian datasets from MPI-AMRVAC and compatible AGILE snapshots, preserving the native AMR hierarchy and connecting complementary scientific diagnostics within a common numerical representation. The framework combines Python workflow interfaces with compiled Cython kernels, supporting efficient analysis on AMR meshes. We compare native AMR analysis with a VTK point-data conversion and uniform-grid resampling, which shows that changes in data association, interpolation support, and differentiation scale affect both sampled magnetic fields and derived current densities. Small differences in the sampled primary field can become more pronounced in derivative-based quantities, particularly near coarse-fine interfaces. The applications combine field diagnostics, tracing, regional statistics, and line-of-sight integration on the same native AMR representation. simesh makes these operations available through reusable Python interfaces for reproducible analysis of multiscale simulation data.

papers.title: Orientation-dependent sensitivity of the all-sky all-frequency gravitational-wave radiometer search to continuous-wave sources
papers.abstract: The all-sky all-frequency (ASAF) gravitational-wave radiometer search cross-correlates the data of two detectors with equal weight on the $+$ and $\times$ tensor polarizations. This is optimal for an unpolarized stochastic background, but not for continuous-wave (CW) sources, whose polarization depends on the inclination angle $\iota$ and the polarization angle $\psi$. Unless the source is seen face-on, the search measures less power than a face-on source with the same intrinsic amplitude, and underestimates its strength. The ratio of the two powers, the projection factor $\mu^2(\iota,\psi)$, is known from earlier radiometer studies. We show how $\mu^2$ enters the ASAF statistic, derive its exact dependence on $\psi$, and prove that its average over orientations is exactly $2/5$, independent of sky position, baseline geometry, noise weighting, and frequency. We apply the formalism to four simulated pulsar signals at four sky positions, with polarization from circular to nearly linear, injected into the LIGO detectors during the second observing run (O2). A nearly edge-on injection is measured with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of $5.20$, below the threshold of $6.19$, while the same signal seen face-on would have an SNR of $31.1 \pm 6.0$. Bayesian upper limits on the strain amplitude $h_0$, marginalized over orientation and calibration uncertainty, are $2.7$ to $2.9$ times the face-on values. For the $505$ sub-threshold candidates of the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run (O4a), the upper limits increase by a factor of $2.5$ to $2.9$, and a source of the same strength would reach threshold only when inclined by less than $34.7^{\circ}$ to $50.3^{\circ}$ from face-on. The measured SNR and the significance of every candidate are unchanged.

papers.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Short-Term Atmospheric Seeing Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. While Gaussian Processes provide a useful probabilistic baseline, their predictive distributions are limited by the Gaussian assumption. FloTS combines competitive forecasting accuracy with flexible uncertainty quantification and produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.

papers.title: A Broadband Room-Temperature Design for the Einstein Telescope
papers.abstract: The unique underground location of the Einstein Telescope (ET) is expected to substantially suppress seismic and gravity-gradient noise, providing a favorable environment for gravitational-wave detection at low frequencies compared with surface-based observatories. The baseline ET design aims to achieve broadband sensitivity through a xylophone configuration, in which separate cryogenic and room-temperature interferometers are optimised for low- and high-frequency gravitational-wave detection. However, achieving the target low-frequency sensitivity introduces substantial technical complexity caused by vertical suspension thermal noise, vibrations of the cryocooler, and detuned optical configuration. In this paper, we demonstrate an alternative, entirely room-temperature, fully resonant, single-interferometer architecture that addresses these challenges and achieves broadband sensitivity superior to that of the conventional ET xylophone configuration. Using mature fused-silica suspension technology, recent advances in optical coatings, and novel inertial isolation, we show that 4-m-long fused-silica fibres can meet the required suspension thermal-noise performance. We further demonstrate that vibrations, optical rigidity, and quantum back-action noise can be controlled through appropriate design of the interferometer, test mass suspensions, optical seismometers, and quantum states.

papers.title: A Catalog of Dispersive Ionospheric and Plasmaspheric Arcs from Cislunar and Lunar-surface GNSS Radio Occultations
papers.abstract: This dataset is a catalog of 263 dispersive arcs induced by ionospheric and plasmaspheric occultation observed in GNSS signals recorded by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE) payload during Blue Ghost Mission 1 (BGM1), in cislunar space and on the lunar surface. Occultation arcs are identified and classified as ingress, egress or tangent by combining independently GPS and Galileo dual-frequency observables and computing the rate of the total electron content (ROT) and ROT index (ROTI), and are validated through a geometric criterion based on the grazing altitude of the tangent point. No distinction is made between the ionospheric and plasmaspheric contributions to each arc, which is treated as a single dispersive signature. For each arc, the catalog provides timing, grazing altitude, summary ROT/ROTI/$\Delta$STEC attributes, the geomagnetic activity level, and time series of leveled slant total electron content (STEC), not corrected for instrumental biases, ROT, ROTI, tangent-point position and local time. The HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format version 5) file contains a header with dataset-wide metadata and per-class statistics, and one entry per arc. It enables rapid selection of occultation arcs for statistical studies and targeted analyses, and complements ground-based and low Earth orbit radio-occultation data during the declining phase of solar cycle 25.

papers.title: Exploring the origin of slow-rotating pulsars: Emission from STARS simulated white dwarfs
papers.abstract: An increasing number of slow-rotating pulsars and long-period transients have been observed in recent years. The periods of these sources can be significantly longer than typical pulsar sources, ranging from ~ 100 - 1000 s, or even longer. The observed periods and period derivatives predict high magnetic fields, higher than the Schwinger field, when we consider conventional pulsar models of dipole-driven emission from neutron stars. Interestingly, the periods of these sources are consistent with the current observations of white dwarfs (WDs). We explore the possibility of magnetic WDs, simulated using the stellar evolution code STARS, as the origin of some of these unusual pulsar observations. We simulate WDs with enhanced magnetic fields due to accretion after their formation. We also briefly touch on the more exotic possibility of super-Chandrasekhar WDs as the origin for these sources. We find that expanding the parameter space to include the possibility of a WD origin provides an alternate and viable explanation for these unusual observations.

papers.title: Saturation Level of the Streaming Instability
papers.abstract: In proto-planetary disks, gas turbulence can cluster dust grains and catalyze the formation of planetesimals. This process depends on the strength of the turbulence. Here, we evaluate the turbulence strength that is induced by the streaming instability. Based on the amount of free energy available, we estimate the viscous parameter to be alpha ~ St Pi^2 f(epsilon), where St (< 1) is the Stokes number of the streaming grains, Pi is the dimensionless pressure gradient, and f (epsilon) is an explicit function of epsilon, the local dust-to-gas density ratio. This estimate explains the results of many previous studies, and is also supported by our additional tailor-made simulations. We discuss two easy applications of our result, one is a self-consistent dust scale height, one is the astrophysical relevance of a pressure bump. Lastly, while this work allows one to characterize the streaming turbulence, we emphasize our current inability to connect the strength of turbulence to the formation of planetesimals.

papers.title: A combined HST and JWST analysis of the stellar population in Draco II
papers.abstract: Draco II (Dra II) is one of the faintest and most metal-poor Milky Way satellites known, yet its nature as either an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy or an extended globular cluster remains debated. We perform a photometric analysis of the stellar population of Dra II reducing deep multi-band observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We select Dra II member stars based on their proper motions and photometric quality criteria. For the first time, optical and infrared photometry are combined to produce a stellar catalogue reaching 50 percent completeness at $F814W = 26.5$ mag (corresponding to the absolute magnitude $M_{F814W} = 10.1$ mag). The colour-magnitude diagram confirms that Dra II hosts an old stellar population with an age of $13.5_{-1.5}^{+1.7}$ Gyr at a distance of $19.2\pm0.9$ kpc. We measure an $\alpha$-enhanced stellar population with a low mean metallicity of $[\rm Fe/H]_{CaHK} = -2.38 \pm 0.17$ dex and confirm the presence of an intrinsic metallicity spread of $\sigma_{[\rm Fe/H]} = 0.85 \pm 0.13$ dex. We identify 10 unresolved main-sequence binary stars in the HST catalogue with mass ratios $q > 0.5$ in the mass range $0.43<M_1/M_\odot<0.71$, corresponding to a binary fraction of $f_{bin}^{q>0.5} = 0.21 \pm 0.07$. This value is higher than those typically observed in globular clusters and lies near the upper range measured in open clusters. The stellar mass function is best modelled by a single power law with a slope of $1.53\pm0.26$ over the mass range $0.13$--$0.77\ M_\odot$. We find no evidence of mass segregation. Consistent results are obtained independently from the JWST catalogue. Combining these findings strongly suggests that Draco II is best classified as an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy rather than a globular cluster.

papers.title: Ammonia Fitting of Multiple Velocity Components in High-Mass Star-Forming Regions
papers.abstract: We perform a multiple velocity component analysis of ammonia (NH$_3$) gas from KEYSTONE, a Green Bank Telescope survey covering 11 giant molecular clouds (GMCs) at distances from 0.7 to 2.7 kpc. We extend existing codes to enable simultaneous fitting of up to three velocity components in NH$_3$ (1,1) with radiative transfer. Using our multiple component fitting technique, we produce the best maps of the centroid velocity and velocity dispersion in these clouds to date. Over the entire survey, multiple velocity components were seen in 13% of pixels where we detect and fit NH$_3$ emission, primarily in clusters at the heart of the GMCs. In these multiple component pixels, the median measured NH$_3$ linewidth decreased by a factor of 1.4 compared to equivalent single-component measurements, but there are also significant cloud-to-cloud variations. Regions with multiple velocity components tend to be found in the densest zones of the GMCs and at the sites of high-mass star formation, indicative of multiple filaments, cores, or complex velocities associated with the formation of massive stars. Disentangling these velocity features will allow future quantitative analysis of coherent motions, such as infall and outflow, in these complex environments. The multi-component data products are available on the CADC.

papers.title: FAUST XXXII. Chemically layered structures and ionisation in the disk and envelope of NGC 1333 IRAS 4C
papers.abstract: Recent molecular line observations with high spatial resolutions have revealed vertical chemical stratification in Class I/II disks (i.e. chemical composition changing with height in the vertical direction of the disk), as well as a radial variation of ionisation rates. However, such chemical layered structures in Class 0 disk and envelope systems have been investigated only for limited objects, such as L1527. In the context of the ALMA Large Program FAUST, we report the results of molecular line observations toward the disk and envelope around the low-mass Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS 4C in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. Previous observations have shown that the disk rotation axis of this object is largely tilted to the line of sight, making it suitable for studying the molecular abundance distribution as a function of disk height. We found that the molecules known as gas density tracers such as C18O and H2CO are distributed around the disk midplane. In addition, molecules known as tracers of photochemical reactions such as CCH and c-C3H2 are distributed in the low-density upper layers of the disk, unlike the distribution in L1527. Moreover, the column density ratio of HCO+/CO derived from the H13CO+ and C18O line emission suggests that the ionisation degree and the ionisation rate vary with the disk radius and they are larger in the outer region of the disk and envelope.

papers.title: White dwarf pollution in wide binaries I: the effects of stellar evolution
papers.abstract: Context. Atmospheric pollution in white dwarfs is interpreted as evidence for the accretion of rocky material from remnant planetary systems. Wide binary companions can influence the delivery of planetary material onto white dwarfs, making it essential to understand the interplay between stellar evolution and binary perturbations. Aims. We investigate how uncertainties in stellar mass-loss histories affect the dynamical evolution of remnant planetary systems in wide binaries, and assess their relative importance compared with binary perturbations in driving the accretion of rocky material onto white dwarfs. Methods. We perform REBOUND N-body simulations incorporating time-dependent stellar parameters interpolated from MESA evolutionary tracks and tidal interactions, following the dynamical evolution up to the white dwarf stage. We explore two stellar-evolution models with distinct mass-loss histories for wide binary systems hosting a Jupiter-mass planet and a planetesimal disc, spanning a range of binary architectures. Results. The adopted stellar-evolution model has only a minor effect on the survival of the planet, mainly affecting the timing and efficiency of planetesimal delivery during the white dwarf stage. Instead, the architecture of the binary primarily controls the pollution outcome: wider binaries produce the highest rates of accretion onto the white dwarf, consistent with the observed prevalence of polluted white dwarfs in wide binaries. Moreover, planetesimal reservoirs remain long-lived, with survival times increasing with binary separation, enabling Gyr-long metal pollution. Conclusions. Our results suggest that the architecture of wide binaries, rather than uncertainties in stellar evolution, is the dominant factor controlling the dynamical delivery of rocky material onto white dwarfs.

papers.title: Hybrid Stars with a Crossover Equation of State
papers.abstract: The possible occurrence of a phase transition in superdense nuclear matter remains an open problem in nuclear physics. In particular, the transition from purely hadronic matter to the hypothesized deconfined quark matter is a subject of considerable interest. Beyond its fundamental significance, this transition has important implications for the physics of compact objects, including neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars. The conventional approaches to this problem involve the Maxwell and Gibbs constructions, both of which have been extensively studied and applied. In the present study, we focus on a third, alternative approach based on a smooth transition from hadronic to quark matter through the so-called switching function. More specifically, the present work focuses on two main objectives. The first is to systematically investigate the influence of the symmetry energy on the transition densities and chemical potentials associated with the transition to quark matter. Subsequently, we attempt to physically constrain and parametrize the two parameters characterizing the switching function, ensuring that the transition from hadronic to quark matter is not merely continuous but also consistent with relevant physical requirements. The main conclusion is that, with an appropriate choice of the aforementioned parameters, the phenomenological model becomes more physically motivated and can serve as a useful tool for investigating the structure and properties of hybrid compact objects. Moreover, this approach offers the flexibility to predict the properties of compact objects that lie beyond the scope of standard neutron-star theory, such as objects characterized by relatively low masses and small radii, which have recently attracted considerable attention in observational studies.

papers.title: Ballistic mixing: stellar mergers drive internal mixing in extremely massive stars, with implications for proto-globular cluster pollution
papers.abstract: Extremely massive stars, with masses of $10^3$-$10^4$ M$_\odot$, have been proposed as potential sources of the chemical enrichment associated with multiple populations in globular clusters. Early on the main sequence, these stars reach central temperatures of 65 to 75 MK, enabling nucleosynthesis through the CNO, NeNa, and MgAl cycles, producing abundance patterns similar to those observed in the so-called cluster's second population. Stellar mergers are among the leading formation channels for extremely massive stars. In this work, we follow the formation of a $\sim6700$ M$_\odot$ star via 253 stellar mergers, drawn from a direct $N$-body star cluster simulation with properties similar to the densest star clusters observed at redshift $z\sim10$. We evolve each star as a 1D stellar model and construct the merger products from mixing and shock heating prescriptions calibrated to 3D simulations of parabolic collisions. We find that entropy-based mixing efficiently transports nuclear-processed material from the convective core to the envelope, while merger-driven heating promotes chemical homogenization. As a result, the stellar surface becomes enriched with H-burning products, producing abundance patterns consistent with those observed in globular cluster multiple populations and supporting the role of merger-formed extremely massive stars as potential sources of early chemical enrichment in proto-globular cluster-like conditions.

papers.title: An Implicit Conservative Finite Volume Scheme with Poisson Brackets for the Steady-State Transport of Galactic Cosmic Rays
papers.abstract: Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) pose a persistent radiation hazard to astronauts and spacecraft in the heliosphere. Modeling their transport is essential for understanding how the solar wind and heliospheric magnetic field shape their spatial distributions and energy spectra. Timely predictions require solving for the particle distribution function much faster than real time, but explicit numerical schemes are restricted by the stability limit on the time step. In this Letter, we present an implicit conservative finite-volume scheme for kinetic equations formulated with Poisson brackets. This scheme conserves particle number, maintains the total-variation-diminishing property, achieves second-order spatial accuracy, and remains stable for time steps far beyond the explicit limit, while reaching quasi-steady states in less than ~1/100 of the computational time required for the explicit scheme, as demonstrated by numerical tests. We apply this scheme to the Parker transport equation along magnetic field lines in the background solar wind during Carrington rotation 2211, where it reaches steady-state GCR distributions within 10 iterations, about 1000 times faster than the explicit scheme. The GCR proton spectrum averaged over 27 days agrees with AMS-02 measurements to within 10%. The simulation also yields a realistic radial intensity gradient and captures the Forbush decrease features associated with three stream interaction regions observed at Earth.
